title: Ordering fractions and decimals
cover_sub: Compare and order decimals, fractions and percentages, including negative numbers, using place value and common denominators.

parents.listen: Ask: can you make them all the same type first? The most common mistake is thinking a decimal with more digits is bigger (0.125 is smaller than 0.5). Writing the decimals with the same number of digits helps.

levels_long.d: Getting the basics: one step at a time.
levels_long.s: Year 8 standard: a few steps, some in context.
levels_long.e: A stretch: problems, reasoning and spotting mistakes.

briefing: To compare decimals, line up the decimal points and give them the same number of decimal places by adding zeros. Then compare digit by digit from the left.
To compare fractions, either change them to decimals (divide the top by the bottom) or give them a common denominator.
Useful facts: 12 = 0.5, 14 = 0.25, 34 = 0.75, 15 = 0.2, 18 = 0.125, 13 = 0.333…
< means is less than; > means is greater than. For negative numbers, the further below zero, the smaller the number.

examples.question: Put in order, smallest first: 0.4, 0.35, 0.405, 0.04
steps: Now compare them like whole numbers: 40, 350, 400, 405.

examples.question: Put in order, smallest first: 35, 0.58, 23, 62%
steps: Write them in their original form.
examples.answer: 0.58, 35, 62%, 23

examples.question: Which is bigger, 58 or 712?
steps: Common denominator 24: 58 = 1524 and 712 = 1424.

d.blurb: Warm up. One step at a time.

text: Write 34 as a decimal.
Which is bigger, 13 or 14?
questions.working: Thirds are bigger pieces than quarters.

s.blurb: The Year 8 standard. Show each step.

questions.tip: Add zeros so every number has 3 decimal places, then compare.

text: Put in order, smallest first: 25, 0.35, 38
questions.answer: 0.35, 38, 25

text: Put in order, smallest first: 0.6, 58, 0.65
Write < or > in the box: 45 ☐ 0.85
Put in order, largest first: 72%, 0.7, 34, 0.705
Write a decimal that is between 0.3 and 0.31.
questions.answer: Any decimal between them, for example 0.305
questions.working: 0.300 and 0.310: anything from 0.301 to 0.309 works, and so do longer decimals.

e.blurb: Problems, reasoning and one piece of tampered evidence.

text: Put in order, smallest first: 56, 79, 45
questions.answer: 79, 45, 56

text: Put in order, smallest first: −0.3, −0.03, −14, 0.2
questions.working: −14 = −0.25. The further below zero, the smaller.

text: Kai says 0.125 is bigger than 0.5. Find the mistake in his reasoning.
questions.working: He compared the digits as whole numbers. Line up the decimal places: 0.125 against 0.500.
questions.tampered:
125 is bigger than 5,
so 0.125 is bigger than 0.5

text: Write a fraction that lies between 13 and 12. Show how you know it does.
questions.answer: For example 512 or 25
questions.working: 13 = 412 and 12 = 612, so 512 is between them. (25 = 0.4 also works.)

mistakes: Thinking more digits means bigger: 0.405 is less than 0.45.
Comparing fractions by their denominators only, so 14 looks bigger than 13.
Ordering negative numbers as if they were positive: −0.3 is smaller than −0.03.
Ordering largest first when the question asks for smallest first.
closed_points: Compare fractions using decimals or a common denominator.
Order a mix of fractions, decimals and percentages.
